title: Docker Compose: The Multi-Container Handbook
summary: A dense field guide to Docker Compose — from the service model and startup ordering to healthchecks, networks, volumes, env resolution, override layering, and horizontal scaling. Covers the mechanics underneath each keyword, the trade-offs, and the mistakes that bite in production.

chapters.title: What Compose Actually Is
points: Definition: Compose is a spec + CLI that turns one declarative YAML file into a set of Docker API calls — it creates networks, volumes, and containers; it is not a runtime or an orchestrator
The unit of work is the *project*: a name (default = directory name) that namespaces every resource it creates, e.g. project `shop` makes container `shop-web-1`, network `shop_default`
Set project name explicitly with `-p myproj`, `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`, or top-level `name:` in the YAML — otherwise renaming your folder orphans your volumes
Compose V1 (Python, `docker-compose`, hyphen) is EOL; V2 is a Go plugin invoked as `docker compose` (space). V2 also dropped the implicit `_` separator: `proj_web_1` became `proj-web-1`
The `version:` top-level key is obsolete in the Compose Specification — Compose V2 ignores it and warns. Delete it
Minimal file: `services:` is the only required top key; `networks:`, `volumes:`, `configs:`, `secrets:` are optional top-level declarations
Compose is declarative-with-reconciliation: `docker compose up` diffs desired state vs running containers and only recreates what changed (image, env, ports, mounts)

Key commands: `up -d` (create+start), `down` (stop+remove containers/networks), `down -v` (also removes named volumes — destructive), `ps`, `logs -f`, `exec`, `run --rm`, `config` (render merged file)
`docker compose config` is the debugging tool that matters: it prints the fully merged, variable-interpolated YAML Compose will actually act on
Example: `services: { web: { image: nginx, ports: ["8080:80"] } }` — 3 lines is a valid Compose file

chapters.title: The Service Block: Anatomy
points: A service is a *template* for containers, not a single container — `scale` makes N containers from one service definition
`image:` pulls a prebuilt image; `build:` builds from a Dockerfile. Both together = build, then tag the result with the `image:` name
`build:` long form: `context`, `dockerfile`, `args` (build-time only, become Dockerfile `ARG`), `target` (multi-stage stage name), `cache_from`
Build args ≠ env vars: `args` exist only during build and never appear in the running container's environment
`command:` overrides the image's CMD; `entrypoint:` overrides ENTRYPOINT. Setting `entrypoint:` resets the image's CMD to empty — a classic silent breakage
`ports: "8080:80"` publishes host→container (short form `HOST:CONTAINER`); `expose:` is documentation only and does nothing on a user-defined network
Always quote port mappings: `56:56` is parsed as YAML sexagesimal and becomes `3416`. Quoting avoids it
`restart:` policies — `no` (default), `on-failure[:N]`, `always`, `unless-stopped`. `always` restarts on daemon boot; `unless-stopped` does not if you manually stopped it
`working_dir`, `user` (`"1000:1000"`), `hostname`, `init: true` (PID 1 reaper for zombie processes), `stop_grace_period: 30s`, `stop_signal: SIGINT`
`profiles: ["debug"]` keeps a service out of the default `up` until you pass `--profile debug` — the clean way to ship optional tooling in the same file
`deploy.resources.limits` (`cpus`, `memory`) is honored by Compose V2 outside Swarm; `deploy.replicas` is honored too, but most other `deploy` keys are Swarm-only and silently ignored

chapters.title: depends_on: Ordering, and Its Big Lie
points: Short form `depends_on: [db]` only guarantees *start order* — Compose starts `db`'s container before `web`'s. It says nothing about whether Postgres is accepting connections
The consequence: your app boots in 300ms, the database takes 8s, the app crashes with 'connection refused'. depends_on did exactly what it promised and you still lost
Long form fixes it: `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }` — Compose blocks until `db`'s healthcheck reports healthy
Three conditions: `service_started` (default, weak), `service_healthy` (requires a healthcheck on the dependency), `service_completed_successfully` (dependency exits 0 — for migration/seed jobs)
`required: false` (Compose 2.20+) makes a dependency optional — if the service isn't in the current profile set, `up` proceeds instead of erroring
depends_on also controls *shutdown* order (reverse) and is transitive: `docker compose up web` implicitly starts the whole dependency graph
Circular dependencies are a hard error at parse time — Compose refuses to build a startup order it cannot topologically sort
Migration pattern: `migrate` service with `condition: service_completed_successfully` on `db: service_healthy`, then `web` depends on `migrate` completing
depends_on has no effect across separate Compose projects or on `docker compose run` unless dependencies are enabled (`run` starts deps by default; `--no-deps` skips them)
The robust belt-and-braces answer: healthcheck conditions in Compose *plus* connection-retry logic in the app. Compose handles boot; retries handle mid-life restarts, which depends_on cannot

chapters.title: Healthchecks: How Compose Knows
points: A healthcheck is a command run *inside* the container on an interval; exit 0 = healthy, exit 1 = unhealthy. Docker stores the state, Compose reads it
Full block: `healthcheck: { test, interval, timeout, retries, start_period, start_interval }`
`test` forms: `["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost/health"]` (exec, no shell) vs `["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres || exit 1"]` (runs via `/bin/sh -c`, so pipes and `$VAR` work)
`interval` (default 30s) = time between checks; `timeout` (30s) = how long one check may run; `retries` (3) = consecutive failures before status flips to `unhealthy`
`start_period` (0s) is the grace window: failures during it don't count toward `retries` and don't mark the container unhealthy — essential for slow-booting JVM or database services
`start_interval` (25.0+) polls faster *during* start_period, so a container that's ready in 2s is marked healthy in 2s instead of waiting a full 30s interval
States: `starting` → `healthy` | `unhealthy`. A container with no healthcheck reports no status at all, and `condition: service_healthy` on it fails immediately
Worst-case time to detect failure ≈ `interval × retries + timeout` — tune these numbers, don't inherit the defaults blindly
`test: ["NONE"]` disables a healthcheck inherited from the base image; `disable: true` is the equivalent Compose key
The command must exist in the image: `curl` is absent from `alpine` and most distroless images. Use `wget --spider -q`, the language runtime, or ship a static binary
Healthchecks cost CPU on every interval across every replica — a 1s interval on 20 containers is 20 process spawns per second
Docker does NOT restart an unhealthy container by itself. `restart: always` reacts to *exits*, not to health. Only Swarm/Kubernetes act on health status

chapters.title: Networks and Service Discovery
points: Compose creates one network per project by default, `<project>_default`, of driver `bridge`, and attaches every service to it
Service discovery is DNS: Docker's embedded resolver at 127.0.0.11 resolves a service's *name* to its container IP. `http://db:5432` just works — no links, no IP hardcoding
Container-to-container traffic uses the *container* port, not the published host port. From `web`, Postgres is `db:5432` even if you published `15432:5432`
Therefore `ports:` is only for host access. Internal-only services need no `ports:` at all — publishing them is needless exposure
`aliases` give extra DNS names per network; a service is also reachable by its container name and, in the default network, by service name
Custom networks segment traffic: put `web`+`api` on `frontend`, `api`+`db` on `backend`, and `web` physically cannot reach `db`
`internal: true` on a network blocks all outbound external routing — the standard hardening for a database tier
Declaring any `networks:` on a service replaces the default attachment; forget to list `default` and the service loses its old neighbors
`external: true` joins a pre-existing network Compose didn't create (and won't delete) — how two separate Compose projects talk
Scaled services resolve to *multiple* A records for one name; Docker's DNS returns them in rotation, giving crude round-robin load balancing with no proxy
DNS round-robin is not load balancing: clients cache resolutions, connections are sticky, and dead replicas stay in DNS until the container is removed
`network_mode: host` (Linux only) skips the network namespace entirely — ports bind directly on the host, and `networks:` becomes illegal alongside it

chapters.title: Volumes: Where Data Survives
points: Three mount types: **named volume** (Docker-managed, `/var/lib/docker/volumes/...`), **bind mount** (a host path), **tmpfs** (RAM only, gone on stop)
Named volume: `db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data` + a top-level `volumes: { db_data: }` declaration. Bind mount: any path with a `/` or `.` — `./src:/app/src`
Compose namespaces named volumes as `<project>_db_data`; `external: true` points at a volume created outside the project and exempts it from `down -v`
Long syntax is explicit and worth it: `{ type: volume, source: db_data, target: /var/lib/postgresql/data, read_only: false }`
Key asymmetry: an *empty named volume* is pre-populated from the image's contents at that path on first use; a *bind mount* never is — it shadows whatever the image had there
That asymmetry is the `node_modules` disappearing act: `./:/app` hides the image's installed modules. Fix with an anonymous volume on top — `- /app/node_modules`
Bind mounts inherit host permissions. A container running as UID 1000 writing into a root-owned host directory gets EACCES — mismatched UIDs are the #1 volume bug
Bind-mount performance on Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) crosses a virtualization boundary and is slow for many small files; named volumes stay inside the VM and are fast
`:ro` for read-only mounts (config, certs), `:z`/`:Z` for SELinux relabeling on RHEL/Fedora hosts
`down` keeps named volumes; `down -v` deletes them; `docker volume prune` removes anonymous/unused ones. Losing a database to a reflexive `-v` is a rite of passage
`volumes_from` is deprecated in the Compose Spec — use a shared named volume mounted into both services instead
Rule of thumb: named volumes for state (databases, uploads), bind mounts for source code in development, tmpfs for secrets and scratch

chapters.title: Environment Variables: Two Different Worlds
points: Critical distinction: variables that Compose interpolates into the *YAML itself*, versus variables injected into the *container's* environment. They come from different places
`${VAR}` in the YAML is substituted by Compose at parse time from the shell environment and the `.env` file next to the Compose file
`environment:` and `env_file:` set variables *inside the container* and are never visible to YAML interpolation
`.env` is auto-loaded from the project directory (or `--env-file`) and feeds interpolation only — it does NOT automatically populate containers
Interpolation defaults: `${VAR:-default}` (default if unset *or empty*), `${VAR-default}` (only if unset), `${VAR:?error}` (fail with message if unset/empty), `$$` to escape a literal `$`
`environment:` accepts map form `KEY: value` or list form `- KEY=value`; bare `- KEY` (no `=`) passes through from the host shell
`env_file:` loads a file into the container; it can take a list, and later files win. Since 2.24 it also supports `{ path: ..., required: false }`
Precedence, highest first: `docker compose run -e` → shell environment (for pass-through keys) → `environment:` → `env_file:` → Dockerfile `ENV`
`env_file` syntax is NOT shell: no `export`, no command substitution, and quotes are handled by Compose's own parser, not by bash
Never commit real secrets to `.env` — `.gitignore` it, ship a `.env.example`, and prefer `secrets:` (mounted as files under `/run/secrets/`) for anything sensitive
Env vars leak: they appear in `docker inspect`, in `docker compose config`, and in child processes. File-based secrets do not

chapters.title: Override Files and Merge Semantics
points: `docker compose up` auto-loads `compose.yaml` *and* `compose.override.yaml` if present, merging the second onto the first
Filename precedence: `compose.yaml` is the preferred modern name; `docker-compose.yaml`/`.yml` still work. If both exist, `compose.yaml` wins

Explicit chains with `-f`: `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up`. Order matters — later files override earlier ones. `COMPOSE_FILE` sets it via env (separator `:` or `;` on Windows)
Once you pass `-f` explicitly, the automatic `compose.override.yaml` pickup stops — you must list it yourself
Merge rules by type: scalars (`image`, `command`) are **replaced**; mappings (`environment`, `labels`) are **merged key-by-key**; sequences (`ports`, `volumes`, `dns`) are **appended**

Appending is the trap: overriding `ports` doesn't replace the list, it adds — so you get both `8080:80` and `80:80`. Use `!reset` (Compose 2.24+) to clear a key, or `!override` to replace it wholesale
Relative paths in an override file resolve against the *first* file's directory, not the override's own — a frequent surprise in multi-directory setups
`extends:` pulls a service definition from another file or service, letting you share a base without merging entire files. It does not carry `depends_on` or `volumes_from`
`include:` (Compose 2.20+) composes whole sub-Compose files into one project — better than `extends` for modularizing large stacks

Canonical layout: `compose.yaml` = the shared truth; `compose.override.yaml` = dev (bind mounts, exposed debug ports, hot reload); `compose.prod.yaml` = prod (pinned image tags, replicas, resource limits, no source mounts)
Always verify a merge with `docker compose -f a.yaml -f b.yaml config` before deploying — the rendered output is the only reliable source of truth

chapters.title: Scaling Services Horizontally
points: `docker compose up -d --scale worker=5` runs five containers from one service definition, named `proj-worker-1` … `proj-worker-5`
Declaratively, `deploy: { replicas: 3 }` sets a default count that Compose V2 honors without Swarm; a CLI `--scale` flag overrides it
Hard constraint: a scaled service cannot have a fixed host port. `ports: ["8080:80"]` with `--scale=3` fails — replicas 2 and 3 collide on 8080
Two ways out: publish a port *range* (`"8080-8082:80"`) or omit the host port entirely (`"80"`) and let Docker assign ephemeral host ports
The usual fix is neither — put a reverse proxy (nginx, Traefik, Caddy) in front and let it resolve the service name, which yields all replica IPs via DNS
Scaling only works for stateless services. Three replicas sharing one bind-mounted SQLite file will corrupt it; three Postgres replicas on one volume will refuse to start
Worker/queue services scale cleanly because the queue does the coordination — the pattern Compose scaling is actually good at
`container_name:` makes a service unscalable: names are unique, so the second replica cannot be created. Same for a fixed `hostname:`
Scaling down removes the highest-numbered containers; there is no graceful drain, so honor `SIGTERM` and set `stop_grace_period`
Compose scaling is single-host. It has no scheduler, no rolling updates, no rescheduling on node failure — the moment you need those, you need Swarm, Nomad, or Kubernetes

chapters.title: Compose vs Everything Else
points: Compose vs plain `docker run`: Compose is a persisted, version-controlled, reviewable form of the same API calls — plus automatic networks, dependency ordering, and one-command teardown
Compose vs Dockerfile: the Dockerfile builds *one image* (build time); Compose wires *many containers* (run time). `build:` is Compose calling the Dockerfile, not replacing it
Compose vs Swarm: same file format, but Swarm is multi-node with a scheduler, rolling updates, and overlay networks. Swarm reads the `deploy:` block Compose mostly ignores
Compose vs Kubernetes: Compose = one host, minutes to learn, no self-healing, no autoscaling. Kubernetes = a cluster, real scheduling, health-driven restarts, and far more operational surface
Compose vs `podman-compose` / Podman `kube play`: Podman offers daemonless, rootless execution and mostly-compatible Compose support; some `deploy` and network features diverge
Legacy `links:` vs modern networks: `links` is deprecated — user-defined networks give the same DNS resolution plus isolation, and don't leak environment variables between containers
`docker compose run` vs `exec`: `run` creates a *new* one-off container from the service definition (use `--rm`); `exec` attaches to an already-running one
`up --build` vs `build` then `up`: identical result, but `up --build` forces a rebuild every time — expensive in a hot loop; use `--no-build` in CI when images are pre-pulled
`stop` vs `down`: `stop` halts containers and keeps them; `down` deletes containers and networks. Only `down -v` touches named volumes
Honest positioning: Compose is the right answer for local development, CI test environments, and small single-host deployments. Beyond one machine, it's the wrong tool

chapters.title: Trade-offs and Production Realities
points: No self-healing: an unhealthy-but-running container stays in service forever. Compose has no controller loop reconciling health to action
No rolling updates: `up` recreates changed containers, dropping connections. Zero-downtime needs an external proxy plus a manual scale-up/scale-down dance
Single host means a single point of failure — no rescheduling, no node draining, no multi-AZ story
Startup ordering is a *boot-time* guarantee only. If the database restarts at 3am, `depends_on` is irrelevant; only app-level retry saves you
Image tag discipline: `latest` in a Compose file makes deployments non-reproducible. Pin to a digest (`image: app@sha256:...`) or an immutable tag in production
Build-on-deploy is a trade-off: `build:` in production couples deploy time to build time and can produce different images on different hosts. Prefer pre-built, registry-pulled images
Secrets in `environment:` are visible to `docker inspect` and often to logs; the `secrets:` top-level block mounts them as files, which is meaningfully safer
Resource limits are opt-in. Without `deploy.resources.limits`, one runaway container can OOM the host and take the whole stack with it
Logging defaults to unbounded `json-file` — set `logging: { options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" } }` or watch the disk fill
State on a single host means backups are your job: named volumes are not replicated, snapshotted, or backed up by anything Compose does
The pragmatic verdict: Compose's simplicity is a real feature. Use it until you need multi-node or self-healing — then migrate, don't bolt on

chapters.title: Common Mistakes: A Field Guide
points: Trusting bare `depends_on` to mean 'ready'. It means 'started'. Use `condition: service_healthy` plus app retries
Unquoted ports: `ports: [22:22]` becomes `1342` via YAML's sexagesimal rule. Always quote
Connecting to the published host port from inside another container. Use `service:container_port` — the host mapping is irrelevant on the internal network
Bind-mounting over a directory the image populated (`node_modules`, `vendor`, `.venv`) and wondering where it went. Layer an anonymous volume on top
Running `docker compose down -v` on a machine holding real data. `-v` destroys named volumes. There is no undo
Expecting `.env` to reach your containers. It feeds YAML interpolation; use `env_file:` to actually inject it
Committing `.env` with real credentials. Gitignore it; ship `.env.example`
A healthcheck calling a binary the image doesn't have — `curl` in alpine — so the service is permanently `unhealthy` and everything depending on it never starts
Setting `container_name:` and then trying to `--scale`. Names are unique; remove it
Assuming override files replace list keys. `ports`, `volumes`, and `dns` *append*. Verify with `config`, or use `!override` / `!reset`
Leaving `version: "3.8"` at the top — obsolete and noisy in V2
Renaming the project directory and 'losing' the database — resources are namespaced by project name. Pin it with top-level `name:`
Using `restart: always` as a substitute for a healthcheck. Restart policies react to process exit, not to a hung-but-alive process

chapters.title: The Whole Picture, One Page
points: Mental model: **project** namespaces → **services** are container templates → **networks** connect them by DNS name → **volumes** outlive them → **env** parameterizes them → **overrides** re-shape them per environment
The four-line startup contract: `depends_on` orders, `healthcheck` defines ready, `condition: service_healthy` links the two, app-level retry covers everything after boot
Networking in one line: talk to services by name on the container port; publish ports only for host access; segment tiers with custom networks and `internal: true`
Volumes in one line: named volumes for state, bind mounts for dev source, `:ro` for config, and `-v` on `down` is a loaded gun
Env in one line: `.env` and `${VAR}` shape the YAML; `environment:`/`env_file:` shape the container; secrets belong in files, not variables
Overrides in one line: base file + `compose.override.yaml` for dev + `-f compose.prod.yaml` for prod; scalars replace, maps merge, lists append
Scaling in one line: `--scale` works for stateless services with no fixed host port and no `container_name`, fronted by a proxy
Debug loop: `docker compose config` (what will run) → `ps` (what is running) → `logs -f <svc>` (why it died) → `exec <svc> sh` (what it sees) → `docker inspect` (what state it's in)
Production checklist: pin image digests, set resource limits, cap log size, healthcheck every service, no source bind mounts, secrets as files, back up named volumes
Know the ceiling: no self-healing, no rolling updates, one host. Compose is excellent inside those walls and wrong outside them

Smallest complete stack worth memorizing: `db` with a named volume and a `pg_isready` healthcheck; `web` with `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }`, a published port, and `restart: unless-stopped`
